claims.text: Retention or loss of toughness in HEAs is governed primarily by the nature and distribution of secondary phases formed during processing.
Increasing the fraction of brittle secondary phases at grain boundaries reduces toughness.
A predominantly single-phase solid-solution microstructure promotes toughness.
A single-phase solid solution promotes dislocation motion and crack blunting.
Controlled heat treatment or alloying can promote secondary-phase formation at grain boundaries.
Brittle secondary phases at grain boundaries act as crack-initiation sites.
Brittle secondary phases at grain boundaries impede dislocation motion.
Crack initiation and impeded dislocation motion caused by brittle grain-boundary phases reduce toughness.
A single-phase solid solution permits more uniform deformation.
More uniform deformation and crack blunting enhance toughness.
Samples with a larger grain-boundary secondary-phase fraction will have lower Charpy impact energy or fracture toughness than baseline single-phase samples.
Baseline HEAs with a single-phase solid solution and minimal secondary phases exhibit high toughness.
The proposed relationship is expected to hold for HEAs with similar base compositions and processing routes when secondary-phase formation is the primary variable.
The proposed relationship may not apply when toughness is dominated by transformation-induced plasticity or another mechanism.
The magnitude of toughness reduction depends on secondary-phase type, fraction, and distribution.
Failure to observe a significant toughness reduction after increasing the grain-boundary secondary-phase fraction would falsify the hypothesis.
